**Hirschsprung's disease (Aganglionic megacolon):** It is due to congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells in both myentric and meissner's plexus in segment of distal colon due to failure of cranial to caudal migration of neural crest cells during development.
**Causes:**

items.text: Endothelial B receptor gene mutation.
Neural crest cell migration defect.
RET proto-oncogene mutation.

blocks.text: **Symptoms:**

items.text: Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life.
Abdominal distention.
Bilious vomiting.
Constipation.
Failure to thrive.

blocks.text: **Clinical Features:**

items.text: Lack of stool in the rectal vault on digital rectal examination.
Explosive release of gas and stool upon withdrawal of the examining finger (squirt sign).
Chronic constipation in older children.

**Meconium ileus (Option A ruled out):** Associated with cystic fibrosis. Usually involves obstruction in the distal ileum (not colon). X-ray: "Soap-bubble" appearance. NOT typically associated with a narrowed distal colon
**Increased enteric ganglion cells (Option B ruled out):** This would enhance motility, not cause obstruction. In Hirschsprung, the issue is lack of ganglion cells.

**Intestinal atresia (Option C ruled out):** Usually presents with double bubble or triple bubble sign on X-ray, depending on location (duodenal, jejunal, etc.). Often has polyhydramnios in utero. Not typically associated with transition zone in colon

blocks.text: **Basal Electrical Rhythm:** Except in the oesophagus and proximal portion of the stomach, the smooth muscle of the GIT has spontaneous rhythmic fluctuations in membrane potential between -65 and -45 mV. The interstitial cells of Cajal are stellate mesenchymal pacemaker cells with smooth muscle-like features that send long, multiply branched processes into the intestinal smooth muscle, generating the basal electrical rhythm (BER).

The function of BER is to coordinate peristaltic and other motor activity, such as setting the rhythm of segmentation and contraction only during the depolarising part of the wave. Spike potentials superimposed on the most depolarising portions of the BER waves do increase muscle tension (figure below). The depolarising portion of each spike is due to calcium influx, and the repolarising portion is due to potassium efflux.
Acetylcholine increases the number of spikes and tension of the smooth muscle, whereas Epinephrine decreases them.
The rate of BER:

items.text: Stomach: 4/min.
Distal ileum: 8/min.
Duodenum: 12/min.

blocks.text: The BER rate in the colon is about 2/min at the cecum and about 6/min at the sigmoid colon.
**Peristalsis:** Reflex response is initiated by the stretching of the gut wall due to the contents of the lumen.

items.text: **Location:** It occurs throughout the gastrointestinal tract, from the esophagus to the rectum.

**Mechanism:** Stretching triggers circular contraction behind the stimulus and relaxation in front of it. The wave of contraction moves in an oral-to-caudal direction. Propels the contents of the lumen forward at rates of 2 to 25 cm/s.

**Regulation:** Peristaltic activity is influenced by autonomic input but occurs independently of extrinsic innervation. Local stretch releases serotonin, activating sensory neurons that stimulate the myenteric plexus. Cholinergic neurons in the myenteric plexus: In retrograde direction: release substance P and acetylcholine, causing contraction behind the bolus. In anterograde direction: activate the neurons releasing nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), causing relaxation ahead of the bolus (Figure below).

blocks.text: **Functional Integration:** Peristalsis is an example of the integrated activity of the enteric nervous system.
**Mass Movement in Colon:** Coordinated contractions of the colon that propel faecal material towards the rectum.

**Gastrocolic reflex:** The gastrocolic reflex is initiated when food accumulates in the stomach. Distention of the stomach causes motility of the proximal and distal colon. This reflex increases the motility of the colon in response to the stretching of the stomach walls after food intake.

This pushes colonic content into the rectum, stimulating the desire for defecation. Therefore, the urge for defecation is usually enhanced after eating a large meal. This reflex is more pronounced in children. The gastrocolic reflex can be more active in children, often leading to a more immediate urge to defecate after eating. Both hormonal and neural factors mediate the gastrocolic reflex.

While gastrin, a hormone secreted by the stomach in response to gastric distension, plays a role, neural factors also contribute to the reflex. The involvement of the enteric and autonomic nervous systems is significant in mediating this reflex.

**Segmentation:** The enteric nervous system promotes a motility pattern that is related to peristalsis but retards the movement of intestinal contents along the length of the intestinal tract to provide time for digestion and absorption. This is the most common movement of the small intestine. It is characterised by closely spaced contractions of the circular muscle layer. These contractions divide the small intestine into many segments.
The rate of segmental contraction is the same as the frequency of slow waves.

items.text: Duodenum: 18/min.
Jejunum: 15/min.
Ileum: 12/min.

blocks.text: Segmentation contractions effectively mix chyme with pancreatic and intestinal secretions. Two nearby propulsive segments force the chyme toward each other into the receiving segment, which efficiently helps in mixing. They also bring the fresh chyme into contact with the mucosal surface.
Therefore, segmentation movements are also called mixing movements. They help in the digestion and absorption of nutrients.

**Migrating Motor Complex (MMC):** Cyclic, recurring motility pattern occurs in the stomach and small intestine during fasting between meals. The MMC occurs during fasting periods between digestion, not during active digestion. Its primary role is to clear the stomach and small intestine of luminal contents in preparation for the next meal rather than facilitating nutrient absorption.
The hormone motilin initiates the MMC. It consists of three distinct phases.

items.text: Quiescent period (phase I)
Period of irregular electrical and mechanical activity (phase II)
Burst of regular activity (phase III).

blocks.text: The MMC contractions migrate aborally (away from the mouth, towards the rectum) at about 5 cm/min, not orally. The MMC occurs at intervals of approximately 90-100 minutes in the interdigestive state.

Gastric secretion, bile flow and pancreatic secretion increased during each MMC. When a meal is ingested, motilin secretion is suppressed, and MMC is abolished until digestion and absorption are complete.

blocks.text: The large intestine (colon) has the longest transit time in the gastrointestinal tract. It is responsible for absorbing water and electrolytes from the remaining indigestible food matter and compacting it into feces. Water absorption and stool formation take longer than other gastrointestinal tract segments.
**Transit Time in Small Intestine and Colon:**

items.text: The First part of the meal reaches the cecum in about 4 hours.
All undigested portions have entered the colon in 8 or 9 hours.
First remnants of the meal traverse the first third of the colon in 6 hours. The second third of the colon in 9 hours and reach the terminal part of the colon (Sigmoid colon) in 12 hours.
From the sigmoid colon to the anus, transport is much slower. 70% of the meal is recovered in stool in 72 hours, but total recovery requires more than a week.

blocks.text: Transit time can be observed by monitoring the progress of a small pill that contains sensors and a miniature radio transmitter.

Receptive relaxation is a physiological process in which the stomach, specifically the fundus and upper portion of the body, relaxes and accommodates food without significantly increasing internal pressure. **Mechanism:** This process is vagally mediated and triggered by the movement of the pharynx and oesophagus.

**Neural Pathway:** The brain responds by sending signals back through vagal efferent fibres, releasing neurotransmitters like nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP). They relax the stomach muscles, allowing them to expand with minimal pressure increase and aiding digestion.

**Subsequent Events:** Peristalsis begins in the lower portion of the stomach, mixing and grinding the food before it passes through the pylorus and enters the duodenum. Contraction of the distal stomach caused by each wave is called antral systole and can last up to 10 seconds. Waves occur 3-4 times per minute. Contraction of the antrum is followed by sequential contraction of the pyloric region and duodenum.

In the antrum, partial contraction ahead of the advancing gastric content prevents solid masses from entering the duodenum. Regurgitation from the duodenum does not normally occur because the contraction of the pyloric segment tends to persist slightly longer than that of the duodenum.
**Adaptive relaxation:** The dilation of the stomach accommodates the food particles that have already entered the stomach. The local vagovagal reflex regulates it.

This is a peptide hormone produced by the liver that regulates iron homeostasis. It inhibits ferroportin, which is the iron transporter on the basal side of the enterocyte, thereby decreasing iron absorption and release into the bloodstream.
**Iron homeostasis:**

**Dietary Iron conversion and absorption:** Most dietary iron is in the ferric (Fe³⁺) form, which needs to be converted to the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form to be absorbed. Gastric secretions and reductase enzymes on the brush border of enterocytes reduce Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺.

**Iron absorption mechanism:** Iron absorption mainly occurs in the duodenum. Fe²⁺ is absorbed by enterocytes via divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) Within enterocytes, some Fe²⁺ is stored in ferritin, while the rest is exported into the bloodstream by ferroportin 1 (FPN1). (Option D) Hephaestin, a ferroxidase enzyme, facilitates the conversion of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ as it is transported across the basolateral membrane.

**Iron transport and storage:** Once in the plasma, Fe²⁺ is oxidized back to Fe³⁺ and binds to transferrin. Transferrin transports iron to various tissues, where it is stored primarily in the form of ferritin and hemosiderin. (Option C)

items.text: **Ferritin:** A soluble protein complex that stores iron safely within cells, particularly in the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and intestinal mucosa. (Option B)
**Hemosiderin:** A more stable and less soluble iron-storage complex found mainly in macrophages, especially under conditions of iron overload.

blocks.text: **Role of Hepcidin: (Option A)** Hepcidin, a peptide hormone produced by the liver, regulates iron levels by binding to ferroportin (FPN1). The binding of hepcidin to ferroportin leads to the internalization and degradation of ferroportin. This process reduces the export of iron from enterocytes, macrophages, and hepatocytes into the bloodstream, thereby decreasing serum iron levels.

Peristalsis is a wave-like muscular contraction that occurs in the smooth muscle layers of the digestive tract, including the intestines. It propels food and chyme forward through the gastrointestinal tract in a unidirectional manner. This is the movement responsible for pushing the contents of the intestine through the digestive system.

blocks.text: Enteropeptidase (also known as enterokinase) is an enzyme secreted by the duodenum, specifically by the brush border cells (enterocytes) in the small intestine. Its main role is to activate trypsinogen (the inactive form of trypsin) into trypsin. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic enzymes that help in protein digestion.
**Enzymes of the gastrointestinal tract (GIT):**

rows: Begins digestion of lipids (mainly milk fat in infants)
Breaks down proteins into smaller peptides
Breaks down lipids, especially in infants
Continues carbohydrate digestion (starches to maltose and dextrins)
Breaks down triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids
Break down proteins into peptides and amino acids
Breaks down nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) into nucleotides
Break down disaccharides into monosaccharides (e.g., glucose, galactose, fructose)
Break down peptides into amino acids
Ferment carbohydrates (fiber) into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and gases

items.text: **Stomach (Option A):** The stomach secretes gastric juice containing pepsinogen (which is activated to pepsin) for protein digestion, but it does not secrete enteropeptidase.
**Jejunum (Option C):** While the jejunum is part of the small intestine involved in nutrient absorption, enteropeptidase is secreted in the duodenum, not the jejunum.
**Ileum (Option D):** The ileum is involved in absorbing nutrients, particularly bile salts and vitamin B12, but it does not secrete enteropeptidase.

blocks.text: Distension of the stomach (i.e., stretching of the stomach wall) is a key factor that stimulates gastric motility. This occurs because the stretch activates mechanoreceptors in the stomach wall, which then trigger the release of signals that promote motility, helping the stomach to mix and propel its contents.

items.text: **Hormones (CCK, GIP, secretin) - Gastrocolic (Option A):** T he Gastrocolic reflex is a reflex that stimulates colonic motility and promotes the movement of feces from the colon to the rectum when food enters in the stomach leading to distension.
**Intestino intestinal (Option B):** When a part of the intestine is over-distended, the rest of the intestine relaxes. This is called intestine intestinal reflex.

**Gastroilea (Option C):** The Gastroileal reflex is a reflex that stimulates the emptying of the ileum, the final portion of the small intestine, by relaxing the ileocecal valve. It is not directly related to gastric emptying or the entry of acidic content into the duodenum.

The Interstitial Cells of Cajal (ICCs) are the pacemaker cells in the GIT, responsible for generating the slow wave rhythms that control the motility of the digestive tract. These slow waves are not action potentials but can trigger action potentials if their amplitude reaches a threshold. When strong enough, they result in rhythmic contractions of the smooth muscle, contributing to peristalsis and other forms of motility.

Serotonin (5-HT) plays a key role in gastrointestinal motility. During peristalsis, stretching of the intestinal wall triggers the release of serotonin. Serotonin activates the myenteric plexus, regulating peristaltic movement.
**Hormones and Enzymes Increasing Gastric Acid Secretion**

**Gastrin (Option A ruled out):** Source: G cells in the stomach antrum and duodenum Mechanism: Stimulates ECL cells to release histamine Directly activates parietal cells to increase H + /K + ATPase expression

**Histamine (Option B ruled out):** Source: ECL cells (in response to gastrin) Mechanism: Binds to H2 receptors on parietal cells Increases cAMP levels, activating H + /K + ATPase to enhance acid secretion

blocks.text: Rice gruel stools are characteristic of cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae infection. The cholera toxin leads to severe watery diarrhea by disrupting the intestinal epithelial barrier and increasing intestinal chloride secretion.

The zona occludens (tight junctions) are crucial for maintaining the integrity of the intestinal epithelial barrier by regulating paracellular permeability and preventing leakage of fluids and electrolytes between epithelial cells. In cholera, the toxin disrupts tight junctions, causing increased permeability and massive loss of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen, resulting in the characteristic watery diarrhea.

items.text: **Gap Junction (Option B):** Gap junctions are responsible for cell-to-cell communication via ionic and metabolic coupling. They are not involved in maintaining epithelial barrier function or preventing diarrhea.

**Adherens Junction (Option C):** These junctions mediate cell-cell adhesion and help maintain tissue architecture. While important for structural integrity, their disruption is less directly linked to diarrhea compared to tight junctions.

**Hemidesmosomes (Option D):** Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the basement membrane and play a role in resisting mechanical stress. They are not involved in regulating intestinal permeability or the development of diarrhea.
